articles.title: Residential Steel Framing: A Guide for General Contractors
articles.audience: General contractors and custom-home builders
articles.purpose: Understand how a GC prices, prepares and coordinates a custom home whose plans specify steel framing.
articles.practicalOutput: A practical GC guide explaining what to review, price and coordinate when the plans call for steel.
articles.scope: The architect and structural engineer usually establish the design and structural system before the GC bids. Focus on pricing and coordinating the specified steel design, preparing the crew and understanding Wheeler’s agreed supply scope. A GC can propose an alternative for the design team to evaluate. Keep detailed training, site logistics and material-cost comparisons brief. Preserve the client’s approved topic and copy direction.

articles.title: How to Compare Custom-Home Steel Framing Quotes in Southern California
articles.audience: Homeowners and builders comparing proposals
articles.purpose: Understand how to compare supplier framing quotations for the same approved home design.
articles.practicalOutput: A comparison table explaining the scope items to align across quotations, how missing work affects comparability and how the homeowner or builder determines an adjusted total from their own quoted figures. No completed quotes or invented prices.
articles.scope: Compare supplier proposals for the same approved home design. Include allowances, exclusions and revisions as worksheet inputs; leave out detailed contract definitions, material-choice comparisons and savings case studies.

articles.title: Insurance for Homeowners in Wildfire-Prone Areas: What to Expect
articles.audience: Southern California homeowners considering a custom home or rebuilding in a wildfire-prone area
articles.purpose: Understand the main insurance issues to investigate before committing to a home design or rebuild.
articles.practicalOutput: An introductory homeowner explanation with the key information to establish before design and procurement decisions.
articles.scope: Orient Southern California homeowners to insurance for the completed home: availability, coverage terms, eligibility and price, and how location, the complete property and construction choices affect the discussion. Distinguish obtaining that policy from settling an existing wildfire claim. Explain a short path from an early conversation with a licensed insurance professional, through identifying relevant construction documentation, to a quotation based on the completed property. Keep claim settlement secondary. Keep detailed discount qualification, calculations, IBHS applications and the full rebuild-coordination timeline brief. Do not promise acceptance, renewal or a framing-only saving. Exclude builders' risk.
questionsForWheeler: Can you share an example of an insurance concern a homeowner raised with you while planning their rebuild?
articles.questionReuseNote: If the previously requested homeowner-insurance case already describes the homeowner’s initial concern, use that answer rather than asking again.

articles.title: How to Qualify for Wildfire Mitigation Discounts
articles.audience: A California homeowner trying to obtain wildfire-related insurance discounts
articles.purpose: Identify applicable program routes, required measures and the evidence to discuss with the insurer.
articles.practicalOutput: A compact program table covering who it applies to, qualifying measures, evidence and how the homeowner requests consideration.
articles.scope: Use current named California programs to explain qualification, required evidence and how to request recognition. For Firewise USA community credit, the insurer verifies the address through its data providers; the homeowner contacts the insurer or agent rather than asking NFPA to verify an individual address. Label insurer mitigation tiers and IBHS designation levels separately even when their names resemble each other. For each percentage used, identify its eligible premium component, policy type and applicable effective-date group; CSAA publishes different bases for different policy groups. A single short, explicitly hypothetical dollar illustration may clarify the premium basis, without becoming a calculation exercise. Include relevant property conditions, such as separation from nearby structures, only as requirements of the named program. Discounts are not automatically additive. Keep detailed IBHS application steps, construction classifications and wood-versus-steel premium comparisons brief. Exclude builders' risk and guaranteed acceptance.
questionsForWheeler: Do you know of a homeowner who applied for a wildfire mitigation discount? What information or evidence did their insurer ask them to provide?

articles.title: How Construction Choices Affect Wildfire Insurance
articles.audience: A homeowner planning fire-resistive construction for a custom home or rebuild
articles.purpose: Understand how a home’s completed construction can affect homeowners-insurance eligibility and premiums.
articles.practicalOutput: A clear explanation connecting construction features, underwriting evidence and conditional insurance outcomes.
articles.scope: Explain how the complete approved construction can affect homeowners-insurance evaluation through named public programs and supported project examples. Use a concrete program requirement to show the link between a design choice, evidence of completed work and insurer review. Where relevant, include separation from nearby structures as a property condition of that program, not a universal construction rule. Explain the different purposes of building approval, product certification, a property designation and an insurer's coverage decision where they affect that example. State the eligible premium component, policy applicability and conditions alongside any figures. A framing material alone does not establish an accepted construction classification or insurance outcome. Keep the market overview, chronological planning, application checklists, IBHS process and steel-versus-wood premium comparison brief.
questionsForWheeler: Can you share an example of an insurer taking a Wheeler home's construction features into account? Which insurer was it, and which features did it consider?
If the insurer offered a discount, how much was it, and did it apply to the whole premium or just part of it?

articles.title: Planning a Wildfire Rebuild Around Insurance Requirements
articles.audience: Homeowners planning a Southern California wildfire rebuild with a design team
articles.purpose: Coordinate insurance-related requirements with the project team while the rebuild design can still be revised.
articles.practicalOutput: A chronological planning guide showing what to confirm, with whom and at which project stage.
articles.scope: Follow the homeowner's planning sequence: discuss intended completed-home coverage and insurer requirements with an insurance professional; bring relevant requirements to the architect and structural engineer; resolve design implications before procurement; collect the evidence the insurer requests; and confirm assessment of the completed property. The architect and engineer normally precede the GC. Make the documentation stage concrete with examples such as the current construction description, relevant plans and evidence of completed mitigation, only as required by the named insurer or program. Distinguish planned features from proof of completed work and revisit relevant requirements when the design changes. Describe coordination using current program information and confirmed business knowledge, without inventing a standard Wheeler insurance-documentation service. Keep the market overview, discount directory, IBHS application checklist and role-based meeting-question guide brief. Stay above construction specifications; compliance does not guarantee coverage. Exclude builders' risk.
questionsForWheeler: On a rebuild you've worked on, have insurance requirements led to a design change? What changed, and when did the team learn about the requirement?
articles.questionReuseNote: Use the same example in the professional insurability article if it supplies that article’s relevant professional question. Do not request another project story merely for a second article.

articles.title: Steel vs. Wood Framing for a Wildfire Rebuild
articles.audience: Homeowners choosing framing with their design team after a Southern California wildfire
articles.purpose: Understand the practical differences the homeowner should evaluate with the architect, engineer and builder.
articles.practicalOutput: A concise wood/steel comparison with concrete implications for the homeowner and a short list of project information needed to evaluate the choice.
articles.scope: Keep the focus on choosing framing for the particular rebuild. Separate material choice from delivery method: steel can arrive as project-specific components for site assembly or as preassembled panels, and wood can also be panelized. Use that distinction only to explain the work, customization or cost information needed for the compared designs. Any public fire example must retain the actual project, observed condition and limits of what it demonstrates. Do not claim steel alone makes a home fireproof, establishes Type II construction or guarantees a cheaper build or policy. Explain material behavior in relation to the home rather than a technical catalogue. Keep whole-property hardening and designation procedures brief.
questionsForWheeler: Thinking of a wildfire rebuild you worked on, what had the biggest influence on the choice between wood and steel framing?

articles.title: Rebuilding After Wildfire: What Homeowners Should Prioritize

Present steel framing's contribution and limits as one possible part of that strategy. Use approved project experience only for the particular observation it supports. Keep insurance applications, detailed budget prioritization and team selection brief. Stay at homeowner decision level without an assembly recipe, an unsupported cost-effectiveness ranking or a survival guarantee.
questionsForWheeler: For the Malibu home where plywood was used instead of the recommended noncombustible decking, what led to that choice?
